title: Internal Website and System Content Defacement via UI or Messaging Modifications
shortTitle: Internal Website and System Content Defacement via UI or ...
summary: This detection strategy covers defacement of internal content, where the goal is not theft but visible damage: an internal portal page, a wiki, a logon banner or a system message is altered so that colleagues see the attacker message. It matters because the same access that edits a web page often reaches configuration that controls banners and system messages, and a defacement is frequently a distraction or a proof of access published while data theft continues quietly elsewhere. The telemetry that makes it visible is file integrity monitoring on web content and static asset directories, content management or wiki audit records showing who published what and when, process creation and file creation events showing the writing process and account, and registry change events for the logon banner and legal notice values. The pattern worth alerting on is a concentrated set of content changes, often with a matching deletion of backups or prior versions, made by an account or process that is not part of the normal publishing workflow. It fails in practice because content platforms are designed to be edited constantly by many staff, so the rule has to model the publishing workflow before it can say that a change is unusual.

beginner.definition: Defacement means changing the content of a page or a message. On the internet this is often a public website. Inside a company it is usually an intranet page, a wiki or a sign in notice. This detection looks for those changes happening outside the normal way of publishing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Defacement damages trust, because staff see that someone reached inside. It is also often a distraction while real theft happens elsewhere. The same access can change the message shown at sign in, which every employee reads. Catching the change quickly limits both the damage and the confusion.
howItWorks: A file watcher records a fingerprint of the files that make up each internal site.
When a file changes, the watcher reports the new fingerprint, the account and the writing program.
The content platform writes its own record when a page is published, edited or deleted.
The detection compares the two views. It checks whether the change followed the normal publishing path.
It looks for many changes in a short time. It also watches banners and system notices.
It checks whether old versions or backups were deleted at the same time.
beginner.example: Think of a notice board in a staff room. Anyone on the communications team may pin a new notice, and everyone expects that. One morning the fire safety poster is replaced with a strange message. The old poster is missing from the bin. The board still looks tidy. Only people who know the routine notice that the wrong person pinned it.
takeaways: Defacement is often a distraction, so look for other activity at the same time.
System banners and sign in notices are content too, and they reach every user.
Baseline who publishes what, or normal editing will look like an incident.

objectives: Explain why internal defacement matters even when no data is stolen.
Identify the content stores, banner settings and message systems that can be altered.
Correlate file integrity alerts with publishing workflow audit records to separate routine editing from abuse.
Recognise the signs of a distraction, including concurrent access to other systems.
Describe the recovery steps that restore content and confirm the scope of the access used.
dataSources: File integrity monitoring on web content directories, static asset folders and template locations
Content management system or wiki audit records showing the account, time, page and action for each change
Sysmon event 11 file creation and modification records naming the process and account that wrote the content
Windows security audit records for object access and registry changes to the logon banner and legal notice values
Web server access and error logs showing publishing requests and the accounts or sessions behind them
logic: Alert when content files in internal sites change in a pattern that the publishing workflow does not explain, weighting mass changes, template and banner edits, and deletions of backups or prior versions. The fields to correlate are the file path, the writing process, the account, the change time and the corresponding record in the content platform audit log. Benign change comes through the platform, by a known editorial account, on one article at a time, during working hours, and usually leaves a visible draft and approval trail. Malicious change typically arrives through direct file writes to the web root, from a service account, a web server process, a scheduler or a scripting host, touches many files at once, includes index pages or templates, and removes prior versions. Registry changes to the logon banner and legal notice are worth separate attention because they display to every user at sign in and have almost no legitimate change frequency. Severity should rise when the defacement coincides with other suspicious activity on the same host, which is common when it is used as cover.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Internal Web Content Rewritten Outside Publishing Workflow
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   content_write:
#     EventID: 11
#     TargetFilename|contains:
#       - '\\inetpub\\'
#       - '\\wwwroot\\'
#   banner_change:
#     EventID: 13
#     TargetObject|contains: 'LegalNotice'
#   mass_change:
#     condition: count() by Image > 50 within 10m
#   filter_publisher:
#     Image|endswith: '\\deploy.exe'
#   condition: ((content_write and mass_change) or banner_change) and not filter_publisher
# level: medium
falsePositives: Marketing and communications teams publishing a scheduled campaign that replaces many pages at once
Site template or theme deployments that rewrite shared assets across the whole internal site
Content platform upgrades or migrations that rewrite files directly rather than through the editorial interface
Static site generation jobs that delete and recreate the published output directory on a schedule
Emergency banner changes made by IT during a major outage, such as a maintenance notice on the sign in page
tuningNotes: Map the normal publishing path first and express it as an allow list covering the accounts, source hosts, processes and times when content changes are expected, then alert on anything outside it. Separate the monolithically published static sites from the interactive platforms, because a build job that rewrites the output directory will otherwise dominate the alert stream. Watch the banner and legal notice registry values separately with a very low tolerance, since these are changed rarely and by few people. Keep the previous version of changed content whenever the platform supports it, so triage can read what was altered rather than only that something changed. The coverage you lose by trusting the publishing workflow is an attacker who uses a compromised editor account to deface through the platform, so pair the rule with anomaly detection on publishing volume per account and with monitoring for sign ins from new locations by editorial accounts.
